notes.text: For more than 8, that's a lot of omelets in a row. Ask another cook to run a second pan next to you.

move.title: Gentle heat, soft eggs
move.body: Heat control means choosing how hot the pan is, and changing it when the food tells you to. Today you'll cook eggs over low heat into a pale, soft omelet, cooked all the way through, and roll it onto the plate like a little log. One omelet per person, one at a time.

why.title: Eggs like it gentle
why.body: Egg is mostly water and tiny strands of protein. Heat makes the strands grab each other and set. Gentle heat lets them link up loosely, so the egg stays soft and tender. Blast them and they squeeze tight, push out water, and turn rubbery and brown.

why.title: Butter is your thermometer
why.body: Watch the butter. Melting means the pan is warming up. Foaming means it's hot enough, because the water in the butter is bubbling away. When the foam settles, pour in the eggs. If the butter turns brown, the pan is too hot.

why.title: Stir, then stop
why.body: Stirring at the start breaks the egg into lots of tiny, soft curds, so the omelet is creamy all the way through instead of one thick layer. Then you stop stirring, so the bottom can set into a smooth skin that holds it all together when you roll it.

why.title: The fastest way to turn the heat down
why.body: A burner takes a while to cool down after you turn the knob. Lifting the pan off the burner cools it right away. Chefs lift the pan for a few seconds whenever the food starts cooking faster than they want.

wrong.sign: The outside is brown and the omelet is rubbery
wrong.fix: The pan was too hot. Turn the heat down a notch for the next one, and lift the pan off the burner whenever it gets ahead of you.

wrong.sign: The eggs stick to the pan
wrong.fix: Wipe the pan clean, use a little more butter, and wait for it to foam before the eggs go in.

wrong.sign: It tore when you rolled it
wrong.fix: Roll it anyway and put the torn side down. It tastes the same. On the next one, let the top set a few seconds longer before you roll.
Slide it back into the pan for 30 seconds on each side, then check again.

quiz.q: The butter in the pan is turning brown. What does that tell you?
choices: It's time to add the eggs
quiz.explain: Brown butter means the pan is hotter than eggs like. Turn the heat down, or lift the pan off the burner for a moment.

quiz.q: Why do you stop stirring after the first half minute?
choices: So the bottom sets into a skin that holds the omelet together
quiz.explain: Stirring makes soft curds. Stopping lets the bottom set smooth, so you can roll it.

steps.text: If you're using chives, rinse them, pat them dry, and chop them into tiny rings. Put them in the small bowl.
steps.tip: Line the chives up in a bundle and slice across the whole bundle at once.

steps.text: Crack all {n:egg} eggs into the medium bowl. Add {qty:salt} salt and a few grinds of pepper.
steps.tip: If a bit of shell falls in, scoop it out with a bigger piece of shell. It works better than a finger.

steps.text: Wash your hands with soap, and wipe the counter where the eggs were.
steps.tip: Raw egg can carry germs. Clean hands before you touch anything else.

steps.text: Whisk until the whites and yolks are one smooth yellow, with no clear streaks of white. Pour the eggs into the liquid measuring cup so they're easy to pour.
steps.look: Even yellow all the way through, with a little foam on top.

steps.text: Put the nonstick skillet on medium-low heat and add 1 teaspoon of butter. Wait for it to melt and foam, and for the foam to start settling down.
steps.look: Small bubbles all over the butter, and it's still pale yellow, not brown.

steps.text: Pour in a little less than ½ cup of the eggs, enough for one omelet. Right away, stir in small, fast circles with the flat of the spatula while you gently shake the pan back and forth.
steps.look: Small, soft curds, like loose scrambled eggs, still a little wet.

steps.text: Stop stirring. Spread the eggs out flat with the spatula and leave them alone until the top is almost set, with just a little shine left.
steps.tip: If the bottom starts to brown, lift the pan off the burner for a few seconds.

steps.text: Tilt the pan away from you. With the spatula, flip the edge nearest the handle over onto the middle. Slide the omelet to the far edge of the pan, then tip the pan over the plate so it rolls out seam side down, like a little log.
steps.tip: Hold the handle with an oven mitt or a towel if it's warm.

steps.text: Slide the thermometer into the end of the omelet, into its thick middle. It needs to read at least 160°F. If it doesn't, slide it back into the pan for 30 seconds on each side and check again.
If any egg stuck to the pan, wipe it out with a paper towel. Add another teaspoon of butter and make the rest of the omelets the same way, one at a time. Check each one with the thermometer.
steps.tip: The pan stays hot between omelets, so the butter foams faster each time. Watch it, not the timer.

steps.text: Turn off the stove. Sprinkle the chives on top if you're using them, and eat the omelets while they're warm.
